hp.hpi:

orders.safety_note: Continuous reassessment is required during shock treatment.

options.text: Flat neck veins with dry mucous membranes and recent vomiting after febrile gastroenteritis.
Crackles, jugular venous distention, and new S3 heart sound.
Fever, warm flushed skin early in the course, and suspected infection.
Sudden pleuritic chest pain, unilateral absent breath sounds, and tracheal deviation.
Hypotension, tachycardia, cool clammy skin, and oliguria.

rows.text: Flat neck veins with dry mucous membranes and recent vomiting after febrile gastroenteritis.
Crackles, jugular venous distention, and new S3 heart sound.
Fever, warm flushed skin early in the course, and suspected infection.
Sudden pleuritic chest pain, unilateral absent breath sounds, and tracheal deviation.
Hypotension, tachycardia, cool clammy skin, and oliguria.

rationale.answer_analysis: Flat neck veins, dry mucous membranes, and vomiting support hypovolemia from volume loss. Crackles, jugular venous distention, and an S3 support cardiogenic pump failure with congestion. Fever, warm flushed skin early in illness, and infection suggest distributive septic shock. Pleuritic pain, absent unilateral breath sounds, and tracheal deviation point toward tension pneumothorax causing obstructive shock. Hypotension, tachycardia, cool clammy skin, and oliguria are nonspecific late perfusion cues that may occur with all four shock patterns. Febrile gastroenteritis can create both volume loss and an infectious source, so this row intentionally maps to hypovolemic and distributive septic shock.
rationale.trap: Do not label every hypotensive client as dehydrated; congestion, infection, and obstruction change the first priority.
rationale.core_concept: Shock recognition requires matching perfusion cues with the mechanism of impaired circulation.
rationale.golden_rule: Treat shock by identifying the mechanism while supporting airway, breathing, circulation, and perfusion.

options.text: Perform and document hourly neurologic assessments.
Add dextrose-containing fluid when glucose reaches protocol threshold while continuing insulin.
Verify potassium replacement parameters before continuing insulin therapy.
Trend lung sounds, work of breathing, and fluid balance during IV rehydration.
Report new headache, bradycardia, rising blood pressure, or decreased level of consciousness immediately.

rows.text: Perform and document hourly neurologic assessments.
Add dextrose-containing fluid when glucose reaches protocol threshold while continuing insulin.
Verify potassium replacement parameters before continuing insulin therapy.
Trend lung sounds, work of breathing, and fluid balance during IV rehydration.
Report new headache, bradycardia, rising blood pressure, or decreased level of consciousness immediately.

rationale.answer_analysis: Hourly neurologic checks and urgent reporting of headache, bradycardia, rising blood pressure, or decreased consciousness target cerebral edema. Adding dextrose at the protocol threshold helps prevent hypoglycemia while allowing insulin to clear ketones, and it also reduces overly rapid glucose decline that contributes to osmotic risk. Potassium verification prevents insulin-related hypokalemia and dysrhythmias. Lung sounds, work of breathing, and fluid balance monitoring help detect fluid overload during rehydration. Fluid-balance trending also helps avoid overly rapid correction and recognizes fluid overload, so that row maps to cerebral edema prevention and fluid overload surveillance.
rationale.trap: Do not stop insulin only because glucose improves; ketosis may still require insulin with dextrose support.
rationale.core_concept: DKA treatment safety depends on controlled correction of glucose, fluids, acid-base status, and potassium.
rationale.golden_rule: In pediatric DKA, neurologic decline is cerebral edema until proven otherwise.

options.text: Boggy uterus that firms temporarily with massage but becomes boggy again.
Firm midline uterus with continuous bright red bleeding and clots.
Placenta documented as incomplete with ongoing uterine bleeding.
Oozing from IV puncture sites with petechiae and low fibrinogen.
Persistent heavy bleeding despite a firm uterus and repair of visible tears.

rows.text: Boggy uterus that firms temporarily with massage but becomes boggy again.
Firm midline uterus with continuous bright red bleeding and clots.
Placenta documented as incomplete with ongoing uterine bleeding.
Oozing from IV puncture sites with petechiae and low fibrinogen.
Persistent heavy bleeding despite a firm uterus and repair of visible tears.

rationale.answer_analysis: A boggy uterus that responds only briefly to massage supports uterine atony. A firm uterus with continuous bright red bleeding points toward genital tract laceration because the uterus is contracted but bleeding continues. Incomplete placenta supports retained tissue and can prevent contraction, so it maps to retained tissue and atony. Oozing from puncture sites, petechiae, and low fibrinogen indicate coagulopathy. Persistent bleeding after the uterus is firm and visible tears are repaired suggests retained tissue or coagulopathy rather than simple atony or laceration.
rationale.trap: Do not assume all postpartum bleeding is uterine atony; a firm uterus changes the differential.
rationale.core_concept: The four T causes are tone, tissue, trauma, and thrombin.
rationale.golden_rule: In postpartum hemorrhage, assess fundus and bleeding pattern together before choosing the next action.

rows.text: Cesarean birth without labor and tachypnea soon after delivery.
Preterm birth with grunting, retractions, and increasing oxygen need.
Maternal fever, poor tone, temperature instability, and respiratory distress.
Sudden unilateral decreased breath sounds with acute oxygen desaturation.
Persistent cyanosis and respiratory distress despite increasing oxygen support.

rationale.answer_analysis: Cesarean birth without labor is strongly associated with retained lung fluid and transient tachypnea. Preterm birth with grunting, retractions, and rising oxygen need supports surfactant deficiency and respiratory distress syndrome. Maternal fever plus poor tone, temperature instability, and respiratory distress supports neonatal sepsis or pneumonia. Sudden unilateral decreased breath sounds and acute desaturation suggest pneumothorax. Persistent cyanosis despite oxygen is a deterioration cue that can occur with severe RDS, infection, or pneumothorax and requires urgent escalation. Preterm respiratory distress can reflect surfactant deficiency, but infection can present similarly; worsening oxygen need keeps sepsis/pneumonia in the differential.
rationale.trap: Do not dismiss neonatal respiratory distress as normal transition when oxygen need is rising.
rationale.core_concept: Birth history plus respiratory pattern helps prioritize neonatal differentials.
rationale.golden_rule: In a neonate, sudden desaturation with asymmetric breath sounds is an emergency.

options.text: Maintain continuous telemetry and immediately report sustained ventricular tachycardia.
Reassess chest pain, ECG changes, and response after prescribed nitroglycerin.
Check blood pressure before giving additional nitroglycerin.
Monitor stool, urine, gums, and puncture sites while receiving antithrombotic therapy.

rows.text: Maintain continuous telemetry and immediately report sustained ventricular tachycardia.
Reassess chest pain, ECG changes, and response after prescribed nitroglycerin.
Check blood pressure before giving additional nitroglycerin.
Monitor stool, urine, gums, and puncture sites while receiving antithrombotic therapy.
Replace potassium per protocol and monitor rhythm response.

rationale.answer_analysis: Telemetry surveillance targets life-threatening dysrhythmias after myocardial injury. Reassessing pain, ECG, and nitroglycerin response evaluates recurrent ischemia, while nitroglycerin can worsen hypotension, so response includes blood pressure monitoring. Checking blood pressure before nitroglycerin directly addresses hypotension risk. Monitoring stool, urine, gums, and puncture sites addresses bleeding from antithrombotic therapy. Potassium replacement addresses dysrhythmia risk because hypokalemia increases ventricular irritability. Sustained ventricular tachycardia is an electrical emergency and can also signal ongoing ischemia after ACS.
rationale.trap: Do not treat chest pain relief as the only ACS outcome; rhythm, perfusion, and bleeding matter too.
rationale.core_concept: ACS care prevents ongoing ischemia while reducing treatment complications.
rationale.golden_rule: In ACS, reassess pain, ECG, blood pressure, rhythm, and bleeding together.

rationale.answer_analysis: New severe headache and vomiting after thrombolytic therapy suggest intracranial bleeding and rising intracranial pressure. Keeping the client NPO until swallow screen completion addresses aspiration risk. Bedside glucose testing addresses hypoglycemia as a neurologic mimic or contributor. Elevating the head of bed and reporting decreased consciousness addresses increased intracranial pressure. Wet cough and desaturation after water indicate aspiration. Decreasing level of consciousness after thrombolytic therapy requires evaluation for increased intracranial pressure and hemorrhagic conversion.
rationale.trap: Do not assume all neurologic worsening is stroke progression; bleeding and glucose changes are high-priority mimics or complications.
rationale.core_concept: Stroke safety includes neurologic monitoring, airway protection, blood pressure control, bleeding surveillance, and glucose assessment.
rationale.golden_rule: After thrombolytic therapy, new headache, vomiting, or neuro decline is hemorrhage until proven otherwise.

options.text: Prepare for early airway support when hoarseness and facial burns are present.
Titrate fluid resuscitation using urine output and perfusion targets while monitoring for worsening airway edema from over-resuscitation.
Perform frequent distal pulse, sensation, pain, and movement checks on circumferential burns.
Use sterile technique during dressing changes and monitor for fever or wound odor.

rows.text: Prepare for early airway support when hoarseness and facial burns are present.
Titrate fluid resuscitation using urine output and perfusion targets while monitoring for worsening airway edema from over-resuscitation.
Perform frequent distal pulse, sensation, pain, and movement checks on circumferential burns.
Use sterile technique during dressing changes and monitor for fever or wound odor.
Administer high-flow oxygen for smoke exposure and elevated carboxyhemoglobin.

rationale.answer_analysis: Hoarseness and facial burns indicate airway edema or inhalation injury requiring early airway planning. Fluid resuscitation guided by urine output and perfusion targets addresses hypovolemic shock from capillary leak. Neurovascular checks on circumferential burns detect compartment syndrome. Sterile dressing technique and fever or wound odor monitoring address infection and sepsis risk. High-flow oxygen addresses carbon monoxide/inhalation injury and also improves oxygen delivery during shock. Fluid titration treats burn shock while avoiding excessive edema that can worsen airway compromise in inhalation or facial burns.
rationale.trap: Do not wait for visible severe respiratory distress before escalating airway concerns in facial or inhalation burns.
rationale.core_concept: Early burn priorities are airway, breathing, circulation, circulation to limbs, and infection prevention.
rationale.golden_rule: In major burns, airway and perfusion can fail before the wound appearance looks worse.

rationale.answer_analysis: Severe headache, hyperreflexia, and clonus are warning cues for eclampsia. Respiratory depression and decreased reflexes suggest magnesium toxicity. Thrombocytopenia, right upper quadrant pain, and elevated AST support HELLP syndrome. Minimal variability with recurrent late decelerations indicates uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal compromise. Calcium gluconate availability and hourly urine output monitoring address magnesium toxicity because magnesium is renally cleared. HELLP reflects severe preeclampsia and therefore also signals increased seizure risk; continued magnesium prophylaxis addresses eclampsia risk while calcium availability and urine monitoring address toxicity.
rationale.trap: Do not confuse therapeutic magnesium effects with toxicity; respiratory depression and loss of reflexes are dangerous.
rationale.core_concept: Severe preeclampsia threatens the brain, liver, platelets, kidneys, and fetus.
rationale.golden_rule: With magnesium sulfate, assess respirations, reflexes, urine output, and calcium gluconate readiness.

rationale.answer_analysis: Wheezing, prolonged expiration, and accessory muscle use support asthma exacerbation. Fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, and focal crackles support pneumonia and can contribute to sepsis when systemic signs appear. Sudden unilateral decreased breath sounds with sharp pain suggests pneumothorax. Hypotension, delayed refill, fever, and altered mental status support sepsis. A silent chest with drowsiness after treatment is a critical fatigue sign in severe asthma, but unilateral silence could also indicate pneumothorax, so both must be considered urgently.
rationale.trap: Do not interpret quiet breathing as improvement when the child is drowsy or hypoxemic.
rationale.core_concept: Pediatric respiratory failure may present as fatigue, reduced air movement, altered mental status, and hypoxemia.
rationale.golden_rule: Escalate any child with worsening mental status and respiratory distress immediately.

Continuous cardiac monitoring primarily addresses hyperkalemia dysrhythmia risk; in an oliguric client receiving urgent treatment, it also supports close monitoring during fluid-sensitive interventions. Hyperkalemia and low bicarbonate together indicate both dysrhythmia risk and metabolic acidosis.
rationale.trap: Do not wait for cardiac arrest before treating severe hyperkalemia; ECG changes are late danger cues.
rationale.core_concept: AKI complications cluster around potassium, fluid, uremic toxins, and acid-base balance.
rationale.golden_rule: In AKI, strict intake/output and cardiac monitoring are safety-critical, not paperwork.

rationale.answer_analysis: Fever, chills, flank pain, hypotension, and tea-colored urine are classic for acute hemolytic reaction. Isolated fever and chills without instability or hemoglobinuria fit febrile nonhemolytic reaction. Urticaria and itching with stable vital signs suggest mild allergic reaction. Acute dyspnea, hypoxemia, crackles, and pulmonary edema during transfusion support a severe pulmonary reaction such as TRALI or TACO. Stopping the transfusion and maintaining access with normal saline is required for any suspected transfusion reaction until evaluated. Fever and chills overlap with febrile nonhemolytic reaction, but flank pain, hypotension, and hemoglobinuria make acute hemolysis the dangerous priority.
rationale.trap: Do not slow the transfusion to see if symptoms improve when a reaction is suspected.
rationale.core_concept: Transfusion reaction management starts with stopping the blood and preserving IV access for treatment.
rationale.golden_rule: Any new fever, respiratory distress, hypotension, flank pain, or urticaria during transfusion is a stop-and-assess event.

rationale.core_concept: Obstructive shock is caused by mechanical blockage to filling or outflow and requires rapid recognition.

rationale.core_concept: Severe drug and skin reactions are distinguished by mucosal involvement, airway symptoms, eosinophilia/organ injury, and infection pattern.
rationale.golden_rule: Airway compromise, mucosal sloughing, hypotension, or altered mentation makes a rash an emergency.

rationale.golden_rule: After neck surgery, airway cues and bleeding cues are priority until proven otherwise.

rationale.trap: Do not focus only on calories; refeeding can become life-threatening through electrolyte shifts.
rationale.core_concept: Eating disorder stabilization requires cardiac, fluid, electrolyte, and suicide-risk surveillance.
rationale.golden_rule: Restart nutrition carefully and treat low phosphorus or potassium as a priority danger cue.

rationale.answer_analysis: A positive pregnancy test with shoulder pain, syncope, and hypotension is highly concerning for ruptured ectopic pregnancy and intra-abdominal bleeding. rationale.trap: Do not rule out ectopic pregnancy because the pain is right-sided or because fever is present.
rationale.core_concept: Pregnancy changes the abdominal pain differential and increases the urgency of bleeding and surgical causes.
rationale.golden_rule: In reproductive-age clients with shock and abdominal pain, pregnancy status is a priority cue.

rationale.answer_analysis: Peaked T waves with potassium 6.4 mEq/L support hyperkalemia. Crackles, jugular venous distention, and acute weight gain indicate fluid volume excess. New confusion with asterixis and severe BUN elevation supports uremic encephalopathy. Kussmaul respirations with metabolic acidosis support acidosis, and severe acidosis can worsen potassium shifts, so it also maps to hyperkalemia risk. rationale.trap: Do not wait for cardiac arrest signs before treating hyperkalemia cues.
rationale.core_concept: AKI causes dangerous retention of potassium, fluid, acids, and uremic toxins.
rationale.golden_rule: Falling urine output is not just a number; it predicts multi-system deterioration.

rationale.answer_analysis: Isotonic fluid improves perfusion and also begins lowering counter-regulatory stress and glucose, indirectly supporting acidosis correction. Insulin treats ketosis and acidosis but drives potassium into cells, so potassium must be reviewed. Adding dextrose while continuing insulin prevents hypoglycemia and permits ongoing ketone clearance; potassium risk remains relevant during insulin therapy. Hourly neurologic checks target cerebral edema. Holding insulin when potassium is low prevents dangerous worsening hypokalemia and dysrhythmias.
rationale.trap: Do not start insulin in DKA without thinking about potassium.
rationale.core_concept: DKA treatment is controlled correction of dehydration, ketosis, and electrolyte shifts while monitoring for cerebral edema.
rationale.golden_rule: In DKA, fluids first, potassium check before insulin, neuro checks throughout.

rationale.core_concept: Major burns threaten airway, circulation, temperature regulation, and infection defenses at the same time.
rationale.golden_rule: Burn care starts with airway, oxygen, warmed resuscitation, sterile covering, and urine-output monitoring.

rationale.answer_analysis: Bag-mask ventilation immediately treats respiratory depression and reduces hypoxic aspiration risk while naloxone is prepared. Side-lying positioning with suction protects the airway and supports inadequate ventilation management. Titrated naloxone addresses respiratory depression while trying to avoid abrupt withdrawal or severe pain crisis. Extended-release ingestion creates recurrent sedation and recurrent respiratory depression risk after naloxone wears off. Agitation, vomiting, and severe pain after a large naloxone dose support acute withdrawal/pain crisis and renewed aspiration risk.
rationale.trap: Do not wait for naloxone before ventilating a severely hypoventilating client.
rationale.core_concept: Opioid reversal is airway-first and titrated to breathing, not to full wakefulness.
rationale.golden_rule: After naloxone, keep watching; the opioid may last longer than the antidote.

rows.text: Administer IV calcium gluconate and continue cardiac monitoring
Give regular insulin with dextrose and recheck blood glucose
Administer nebulized albuterol as prescribed
Prepare for urgent hemodialysis
Repeat serum potassium and ECG after initial therapy

rationale.answer_analysis: Calcium gluconate stabilizes the cardiac membrane but does not lower serum potassium, and monitoring must continue. Insulin with dextrose shifts potassium intracellularly and requires glucose monitoring to prevent hypoglycemia. Albuterol also shifts potassium into cells. Hemodialysis removes potassium from the body and requires ongoing monitoring. Repeating potassium and ECG evaluates cardiac membrane risk, treatment response to shifting therapies, effectiveness of removal strategies, and recurrence.
rationale.trap: Do not assume calcium lowers potassium; it buys time by protecting the heart.
rationale.core_concept: Hyperkalemia treatment has three tracks: stabilize, shift, and remove.
rationale.golden_rule: Treat the ECG first, then lower potassium, then prove the response with repeat monitoring.

rationale.answer_analysis: Droplet precautions reduce meningococcal transmission. Blood cultures followed by timely empiric antibiotics treat suspected bacterial meningitis and sepsis; effective antibiotics also reduce infectious transmission over time. rationale.golden_rule: Protect the public and the brain at the same time: precautions plus prompt treatment.

rationale.answer_analysis: Magnesium sulfate is given primarily to prevent eclamptic seizures and may support fetal safety by reducing maternal seizure-related hypoxia and injury. Monitoring respiratory rate, reflexes, and urine output detects magnesium toxicity. Severe headache and visual changes indicate seizure risk; right upper quadrant pain, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes support severe preeclampsia or HELLP with stroke risk. Nonreassuring fetal status indicates fetal compromise and may reflect worsening placental disease. rationale.trap: Do not treat magnesium as an antihypertensive; it is primarily seizure prophylaxis.
rationale.core_concept: Severe preeclampsia threatens the brain, liver, platelets, kidneys, and fetus.
rationale.golden_rule: Prevent seizures, control severe blood pressure, and monitor magnesium toxicity every time.

rationale.answer_analysis: Fever, chills, flank pain, hypotension, and dark urine support acute hemolytic reaction. Hives and itching without respiratory or hemodynamic instability suggest allergic reaction. Dyspnea with hypertension, jugular venous distention, and crackles supports TACO, though respiratory distress during transfusion also requires differentiation from TRALI. Acute hypoxemia with bilateral infiltrates, hypotension, and no volume overload signs supports TRALI. Stopping the transfusion and maintaining access with normal saline is the immediate action for all suspected transfusion reactions.
rationale.trap: Do not simply slow the transfusion when a serious reaction is suspected.
rationale.core_concept: Transfusion reactions can look respiratory, allergic, hemolytic, or volume-related and require immediate interruption.
rationale.golden_rule: Stop the blood first, keep the line open with saline, then escalate and investigate.

rationale.answer_analysis: Headache, vomiting, bradycardia, and rising blood pressure during DKA treatment are priority cues for cerebral edema. Low potassium with weakness and U waves supports hypokalemia. A glucose of 188 mg/dL with persistent acidosis means hypoglycemia risk is rising while ketosis is unresolved. Adding dextrose allows insulin to continue clearing ketones while preventing hypoglycemia. Holding insulin when potassium is below protocol limit prevents worsening hypokalemia, but it also delays ketosis resolution, so the provider must be notified and potassium corrected urgently.
rationale.trap: Do not stop thinking after glucose improves; acidosis may still be dangerous.
rationale.core_concept: Pediatric DKA treatment requires simultaneous neuro, potassium, glucose, and acidosis surveillance.
rationale.golden_rule: Treat DKA until ketones and acidosis resolve, but never ignore cerebral edema or low potassium.

rationale.answer_analysis: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin after cervical injury supports neurogenic shock. Severe hypertension with pounding headache and bladder distention is classic autonomic dysreflexia. Weak cough, shallow respirations, and rising carbon dioxide support respiratory compromise from high cervical injury. Compression devices and anticoagulant prophylaxis target venous thromboembolism; mobility and pulmonary complications are also linked, so respiratory prevention remains relevant. Frequent blood pressure checks after high thoracic injury screen for neurogenic shock and autonomic dysreflexia, while pulmonary hygiene addresses respiratory compromise.
rationale.trap: Do not treat all post-spinal-injury hypotension as blood loss; bradycardia and warm skin suggest neurogenic shock.
rationale.core_concept: Spinal cord injury complications depend strongly on injury level and autonomic disruption.
rationale.golden_rule: With high cord injuries, protect ventilation, circulation, skin, and clot prevention from the beginning.

Dark bleeding with constant abdominal pain supports placental abruption. rationale.core_concept: Pregnancy pain and bleeding require simultaneous assessment for labor, infection, and placental complications.
rationale.golden_rule: Monitor mother and fetus while escalating bleeding, contractions, or infection cues.

rationale.answer_analysis: Tall peaked T waves and high potassium with weakness support hyperkalemia. Crackles with hypoxemia supports fluid overload. Pruritus, nausea, and confusion are uremic symptoms. Oliguria can contribute to hyperkalemia, volume overload, and uremic toxin buildup, so it maps to all three complications. High potassium with muscle weakness is a hyperkalemia cue, and generalized weakness can also be worsened by uremic toxin buildup.
rationale.trap: Do not wait for chest pain to act on hyperkalemia; rhythm changes can be sudden.
rationale.core_concept: AKI threatens electrolyte balance, fluid status, and toxin clearance at the same time.
rationale.golden_rule: Low urine output plus abnormal potassium or breathing changes is a priority escalation cue.

rationale.answer_analysis: Rapid fever with rigidity supports malignant hyperthermia. Slow respirations with difficult arousal support opioid oversedation. Tinnitus, metallic taste, and seizure cues support local anesthetic systemic toxicity. High end-tidal carbon dioxide can occur with malignant hyperthermia from hypermetabolism or with opioid-related hypoventilation. rationale.trap: Do not assume all PACU hypoventilation is routine sedation when rigidity and rising temperature are present.
rationale.core_concept: Post-anesthesia emergencies are recognized by respiratory pattern, neurologic status, temperature, rigidity, and exposure history.
rationale.golden_rule: Escalate sudden PACU respiratory depression or hyperthermia immediately.

rationale.answer_analysis: Fever, chills, flank pain, and hypotension are acute hemolytic reaction cues. Dyspnea during transfusion can occur with acute hemolytic reactions or circulatory overload; crackles and hypertension make overload especially likely. Urticaria and itching without respiratory compromise supports a mild allergic reaction. Anxiety and chest tightness can appear with severe hemolytic reactions or volume overload. A heart failure history increases risk for transfusion-associated circulatory overload.
rationale.trap: Do not slow the transfusion and watch when a serious reaction is suspected; stop it first.
rationale.core_concept: Transfusion reactions are separated by fever/hemolysis cues, volume overload cues, and allergic skin findings.
rationale.golden_rule: Stop the transfusion immediately for suspected serious reaction and keep IV access with normal saline.

rationale.answer_analysis:
* **Row 1:** (hypotension requiring vasopressors) explicitly defines Septic Shock and serves as a primary driver of MODS, satisfying the 'at least 2 checked columns' rule. 
* **Row 2:** (oozing from IV site and petechiae) represents consumer coagulopathy under DIC, which also manifests as hematological dysfunction within MODS. 
* **Row 3:** (elevated lactate) indicates systemic tissue hypoperfusion across Sepsis, Septic Shock, and MODS. 
* **Row 4:** (elevated creatinine and bilirubin) reflects concurrent renal and hepatic failure, defining MODS.
rationale.trap: Do not wait for blood pressures to drop before identifying sepsis; early microvascular dysfunction begins well before macrovascular collapse.
rationale.core_concept: Septic shock is a subset of sepsis where underlying circulatory and cellular/metabolic abnormalities drastically increase mortality.
rationale.golden_rule: Persistent cellular hypoperfusion leads directly to progressive, sequential organ failure.

Urine output is 45 mL over three hours despite IV fluid administration.

Urine output is 45 mL over three hours despite IV fluid administration.

rationale.answer_analysis: Hypotension with tachycardia supports septic shock because infection plus hypoperfusion is present, and it also supports hypovolemia because poor intake and vasodilation can reduce circulating volume. Minimal urine output despite fluids supports acute kidney injury and hypovolemia; it does not independently prove delirium. Worsening disorientation and lethargy support acute delirium and can also be a sign of sepsis-related hypoperfusion. Elevated lactate with fever and leukocytosis is most consistent with septic shock physiology. Poor intake and orthostatic-type dizziness support hypovolemia and may contribute to kidney injury. Cloudy foul-smelling urine with dysuria supports the urinary infectious source driving sepsis, but it does not by itself diagnose AKI, hypovolemia, or delirium.
rationale.trap: Do not treat confusion in an older adult as baseline dementia when infection, hypotension, or hypoxia is present.
rationale.core_concept: Sepsis becomes shock when infection is accompanied by tissue hypoperfusion, hypotension, or elevated lactate.
rationale.golden_rule: Trend perfusion findings together: mental status, blood pressure, lactate, skin signs, and urine output.

rationale.answer_analysis: Seizure precautions primarily address eclamptic seizure. Hourly respiratory, neurologic, and reflex assessments address magnesium toxicity because respiratory depression, decreased consciousness, and loss of reflexes are warning signs. Severe hypertension increases maternal stroke risk and can worsen uteroplacental perfusion, so antihypertensive therapy addresses maternal stroke and fetal compromise. Thrombocytopenia with right upper quadrant pain suggests severe disease or HELLP features, increasing seizure, stroke, and fetal risk. Lateral positioning and continuous fetal monitoring support uteroplacental perfusion and fetal assessment while also reducing risk during possible seizure activity. Calcium gluconate is the antidote for magnesium toxicity, not a treatment for hypertension or fetal compromise.
rationale.trap: Do not assume magnesium treats hypertension; it prevents seizures and requires toxicity monitoring.
rationale.core_concept: Severe preeclampsia is a multisystem disorder involving neurologic, hepatic, renal, hematologic, and fetal risks.
rationale.golden_rule: Treat severe-range blood pressure promptly while protecting the client from seizures and magnesium toxicity.

rationale.answer_analysis: Initial isotonic fluids restore circulating volume and reduce the danger of rapid osmotic shifts, so they address severe dehydration and cerebral edema risk. Continuing insulin with dextrose allows ketosis and acidosis to resolve while preventing excessive hypoglycemia; insulin also shifts potassium intracellularly, so hypokalemia risk must be anticipated. Potassium monitoring and replacement address treatment-related hypokalemia. Sudden headache or decreased consciousness is concerning for cerebral edema. Urine output must be adequate before potassium replacement to reduce hyperkalemia risk. Avoiding rapid osmolality correction addresses cerebral edema risk and supports safer restoration of volume status.
rationale.trap: Do not stop insulin just because glucose improves; ketone clearance requires continued insulin.
rationale.core_concept: DKA treatment corrects dehydration first, then safely resolves ketosis while closely managing potassium.
rationale.golden_rule: In DKA, potassium can look high initially but fall dangerously once insulin and fluids begin.

rationale.golden_rule: Hold the suspected medication and escalate immediately when hyperthermia and neurologic findings coexist.

rationale.answer_analysis: A boggy displaced fundus with clots indicates uterine atony and ongoing blood loss that can progress to hypovolemic shock. Incomplete placenta and manual removal suggest retained fragments, which can prevent uterine contraction and worsen atony. Oozing from gums and IV sites with thrombocytopenia and low fibrinogen supports DIC. Tachycardia with hypotension indicates hypovolemic shock. rationale.trap: Do not assume all postpartum bleeding is simple atony when coagulopathy or retained tissue signs are present.
rationale.core_concept: Postpartum hemorrhage causes are often remembered as tone, tissue, trauma, and thrombin.
rationale.golden_rule: Quantify blood loss, treat uterine tone, and escalate early when vital signs or clotting signs worsen.

rationale.answer_analysis: Low serum calcium supports hypocalcemia, a known severe pancreatitis complication. Hypotension with tachycardia and clammy skin supports shock from third spacing and systemic inflammation. Hypoxemia with diffuse bilateral opacities supports ARDS. rationale.trap: Do not treat pancreatitis as an abdominal pain problem only; systemic complications can be fatal.
rationale.core_concept: Severe pancreatitis can cause capillary leak, shock, hypocalcemia, ARDS, and renal injury.
rationale.golden_rule: Worsening oxygenation, blood pressure, urine output, or mentation in pancreatitis requires urgent escalation.

rationale.core_concept: Fetal heart changes must be interpreted with contraction pattern, membrane status, bleeding, pain, and obstetric history.
rationale.golden_rule: In labor, sudden severe pain plus fetal deterioration after previous cesarean is uterine rupture until proven otherwise.

rationale.answer_analysis: Pinpoint pupils with severe respiratory depression support opioid toxicity. Dry mucous membranes, urinary retention, flushing, fever, and agitation support anticholinergic toxicity, such as diphenhydramine overdose. Unknown timing with acetaminophen exposure requires serum level interpretation and antidote planning because early liver injury may be silent. rationale.trap: Do not wait for liver enzymes to rise before considering acetaminophen toxicity when timing is unclear.
rationale.core_concept: Mixed overdose requires toxidrome recognition, airway support, ECG monitoring, and early poison control involvement.
rationale.golden_rule: In overdose, stabilize airway and breathing first, then refine antidote and monitoring decisions.

options.text: Decreased urine output, graft tenderness, fever, and rising creatinine after recent transplantation
Severe headache, hand tremor, hypertension, and tacrolimus trough above the expected range
Oral white plaques, fever, and low WBC count while receiving immunosuppressive medications
Potassium 6.1 mEq/L with oliguria and increasing creatinine after kidney transplantation
Avoid grapefruit products and verify new macrolide or azole prescriptions before administration
Initiate cardiac monitoring and obtain stat ECG while notifying the transplant provider

rows.text: Decreased urine output, graft tenderness, fever, and rising creatinine after recent transplantation
Severe headache, hand tremor, hypertension, and tacrolimus trough above the expected range
Oral white plaques, fever, and low WBC count while receiving immunosuppressive medications
Potassium 6.1 mEq/L with oliguria and increasing creatinine after kidney transplantation
Avoid grapefruit products and verify new macrolide or azole prescriptions before administration
Initiate cardiac monitoring and obtain stat ECG while notifying the transplant provider

rationale.answer_analysis:
* **R1:** supports acute graft rejection because graft tenderness, fever, oliguria, and rising creatinine are classic rejection cues; oliguria and creatinine elevation also indicate hyperkalemia with AKI risk. 
* **R2:** maps to tacrolimus toxicity because tremor, headache, hypertension, and a high trough level are consistent with calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity. 
* **R3:** maps to opportunistic infection because immunosuppression with fever, leukopenia, and oral plaques suggests fungal or other opportunistic infection. 
* **R4:** maps to rejection, tacrolimus toxicity, and hyperkalemia/AKI because either rejection or tacrolimus nephrotoxicity can reduce renal potassium clearance. 
* **R5:** prevents tacrolimus toxicity and secondary kidney injury because grapefruit, macrolides, and azoles can raise tacrolimus levels. 
* **R6:** addresses immediate dysrhythmia risk and the two likely kidney-threatening causes: rejection and tacrolimus toxicity.
rationale.trap: Do not assume all post-transplant creatinine elevation is rejection; nephrotoxic immunosuppressant levels and infection can look similar.
rationale.core_concept: Recent transplant clients with fever, graft tenderness, oliguria, high creatinine, and hyperkalemia need rapid provider notification and cardiac safety actions.
rationale.golden_rule: Protect the graft and the heart first: oliguria plus potassium elevation is an emergency until proven otherwise.

rationale.answer_analysis:
* **R1:** maps to tumor lysis syndrome and AKI because chemotherapy-related cell breakdown releases potassium, phosphate, and uric acid, which can damage kidneys and cause dysrhythmias. 
* **R2:** maps to neutropenic sepsis and AKI because fever with ANC 280 is sepsis until proven otherwise, and hypotension can worsen renal perfusion. 
* **R3:** maps to spinal cord compression because back pain with bilateral weakness and urinary retention is a neurologic emergency. 
* **R4:** treats tumor lysis and protects the kidneys by reducing uric acid burden and promoting excretion while monitoring for hyperkalemic dysrhythmias. 
* **R5:** treats neutropenic sepsis; antibiotics should not be delayed for complete diagnostic workups. 
* **R6:** addresses spinal cord compression because neurologic deficits require immediate escalation and protection from further injury.
rationale.trap: Do not wait for a high WBC count in neutropenia; fever may be the only early sepsis cue.
rationale.core_concept: Oncology emergencies frequently overlap: tumor lysis damages kidneys, sepsis reduces perfusion, and spinal cord compression threatens permanent neurologic loss.
rationale.golden_rule: Fever with neutropenia, new neurologic deficits, and hyperkalemia after chemotherapy are all same-shift emergencies.

* **R1:** maps to anastomotic leak with sepsis and possible shock because fever, rigid abdomen, leukocytosis, and lactate elevation after bowel surgery are concerning for leak and systemic hypoperfusion.

* **R5:** addresses leak risk and ileus because NPO and surgeon notification are appropriate for worsening distention and peritoneal symptoms. 
* **R6:** reduces pulmonary embolism risk and promotes bowel motility, supporting prevention of both PE and ileus.
rationale.trap: Do not dismiss tachycardia and pain as routine postoperative findings when oxygenation, drainage, or perfusion are worsening.
rationale.core_concept: Postoperative rescue depends on distinguishing expected recovery from leak, ileus, bleeding, and thromboembolism.

rationale.answer_analysis:
* **R1:** maps to GBS respiratory failure because ascending weakness after infection, areflexia, weak cough, and declining vital capacity indicate neuromuscular ventilatory failure. 
* **R2:** maps to myasthenic crisis because fatigable ocular, bulbar, and respiratory weakness are typical. 
* **R3:** maps to cholinergic crisis because muscarinic symptoms plus weakness after excess pyridostigmine distinguish it from myasthenic crisis. 
* **R4:** maps to autonomic dysreflexia because severe hypertension, bradycardia, headache, flushing above the lesion, and bladder distention are classic. 
* **R5:** maps to both GBS and myasthenic crisis because dysphagia, weak cough, and low vital capacity threaten ventilation in either disorder. 
* **R6:** maps to cholinergic crisis and autonomic dysreflexia because bradycardia and diaphoresis can occur in both; the nurse must distinguish muscarinic excess from severe spinal-cord trigger hypertension before giving additional pyridostigmine.
rationale.trap: Do not wait for oxygen saturation to fall before acting; neuromuscular clients can fail ventilation while SpO2 still looks acceptable.
rationale.core_concept: Forced vital capacity, swallowing, cough strength, and trigger assessment are more important than a single pulse oximetry reading in neuromuscular emergencies.
rationale.golden_rule: Bulbar weakness plus declining vital capacity means prepare for airway support now.

Tearing pain to the back with unequal pressures supports aortic dissection. Shortness of breath and falling saturation may occur with ACS or PE. Severe hypertension with abrupt chest pain can occur with ACS but should also raise concern for dissection, especially with tearing pain or pulse differences.
rationale.trap: Anchoring on one chest-pain diagnosis before comparing the pattern of pain, oxygenation, pulses, and risk factors.
rationale.core_concept: ACS, PE, and dissection can all be fatal and require rapid, differentiated assessment.
rationale.golden_rule: Chest pain plus instability means gather decisive cues quickly and avoid unsafe assumptions.

rationale.answer_analysis: Linezolid plus sertraline is a high-risk serotonergic interaction. Hyperreflexia, clonus, diarrhea, and diaphoresis strongly support serotonin syndrome. Severe generalized rigidity and hyperthermia can appear in neuroleptic malignant syndrome after dopamine antagonist exposure and in malignant hyperthermia after an anesthetic trigger; the medication/timing separates them. Dry flushed skin, urinary retention, mydriasis, and absent bowel sounds are anticholinergic toxicity cues. Rapid hypercarbia and rigidity during anesthesia suggest malignant hyperthermia; rigidity and hyperthermia can overlap with NMS, but the trigger is key.

For each nursing action below, click to specify which goal(s) it supports. Each action may support more than one goal.

options.text: Turn client to side when safe and have suction/oxygen available
Move objects away, pad side rails per policy, and protect head without restraining limbs
Time the seizure and document motor activity, eye deviation, and recovery
Administer prescribed rescue benzodiazepine if seizure exceeds protocol duration
Teach not to abruptly stop antiseizure medication and to refill before running out

rows.text: Turn client to side when safe and have suction/oxygen available
Move objects away, pad side rails per policy, and protect head without restraining limbs
Time the seizure and document motor activity, eye deviation, and recovery
Administer prescribed rescue benzodiazepine if seizure exceeds protocol duration
Teach not to abruptly stop antiseizure medication and to refill before running out

rationale.answer_analysis: Side positioning and suction/oxygen support airway and reduce injury/aspiration risk. Clearing hazards and protecting the head prevent trauma without unsafe restraint. Timing and documentation help determine status epilepticus management and injury risk. Rescue benzodiazepine treats prolonged seizure and protects airway by stopping ongoing convulsive activity, though monitoring for respiratory depression is needed. Medication adherence teaching prevents recurrence.
rationale.trap: Do not put anything in the client’s mouth during a seizure.
rationale.core_concept: Seizure care focuses on airway, injury prevention, timing, and rescue therapy when indicated.
rationale.golden_rule: Time the seizure and escalate if it does not stop.

items.clinical_focus: Iron deficiency anemia teaching

hp.hpi:
Chief Complaint: Fatigue and heavy menstrual periods.
HPI: Hannah Lee reports fatigue, dizziness on exertion, pica for ice, and heavy menstrual bleeding. Labs show microcytic anemia and low ferritin. She is prescribed oral iron and asks how to take it and what adverse effects to expect. The nurse must connect teaching to iron absorption, side effects, and bleeding follow-up.
Relevant History: Heavy menses, vegetarian diet, no GI disease known.

notes.note: Client states she usually takes supplements with tea and calcium tablets at breakfast.

labs.clinical_relevance: Anemia severity monitoring.
Supports iron deficiency.

orders.order: Oral iron, nutrition teaching, constipation prevention, and follow-up evaluation of heavy bleeding.
orders.safety_note: Keep iron away from children; overdose is dangerous.

options.text: Take iron with vitamin C or orange juice if tolerated
Avoid taking iron at the same time as calcium supplements, tea, or antacids
Expect dark stools and report severe abdominal pain or signs of GI bleeding
Increase fluids/fiber if constipation occurs and use stool softener if prescribed
Follow up for heavy menstrual bleeding evaluation and report worsening dizziness, palpitations, or shortness of breath

rows.text: Take iron with vitamin C or orange juice if tolerated
Avoid taking iron at the same time as calcium supplements, tea, or antacids
Expect dark stools and report severe abdominal pain or signs of GI bleeding
Increase fluids/fiber if constipation occurs and use stool softener if prescribed
Follow up for heavy menstrual bleeding evaluation and report worsening dizziness, palpitations, or shortness of breath

rationale.answer_analysis: Vitamin C improves iron absorption. Calcium, tea, and antacids reduce absorption when taken together with iron. Dark stools can be expected, but severe pain or bleeding signs require follow-up for adverse effects or blood loss. Fluids, fiber, and stool softeners manage constipation. Heavy menstrual bleeding evaluation identifies ongoing blood loss, and worsening dizziness, palpitations, or shortness of breath may indicate symptomatic anemia requiring follow-up.
rationale.trap: Do not ignore the cause of iron loss after prescribing iron.
rationale.core_concept: Iron teaching includes absorption, constipation/dark stools, safety, and source control.
rationale.golden_rule: Treat deficiency and investigate ongoing bleeding.

items.clinical_focus: Post-stroke aspiration, impaired mobility, and neglect

patient.name: Arthur Davis
patient.admission_diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke with left-sided weakness

hp.hpi:
Chief Complaint: Left-sided weakness and slurred speech.
HPI: Arthur Davis is admitted after ischemic stroke. He has left facial droop, dysarthria, left arm weakness, and ignores objects on the left side of the tray. His spouse tries to give him water before swallow screening is completed. The nurse must connect interventions to aspiration, injury/fall risk, and unilateral neglect.
Relevant History: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, former smoker.

notes.note: Client coughs after spouse offers water. He bumps his left arm on the bed rail and does not notice food on the left side of the tray.

orders.order: NPO until swallow screen, aspiration precautions, fall precautions, PT/OT/speech therapy consults.
orders.safety_note: Do not give oral intake until dysphagia screening is completed.

rationale.answer_analysis: NPO status prevents aspiration until swallow safety is evaluated. Placing items on the unaffected side maintains access and safety while scanning teaches neglect compensation. Assisted transfers and alarms reduce fall risk. Speech therapy addresses dysphagia and diet safety. Protecting the weak arm prevents injury and supports awareness of the neglected side.
rationale.trap: Do not allow family to give water before swallow screening.
rationale.core_concept: Stroke safety requires aspiration screening, fall prevention, and neglect strategies.
rationale.golden_rule: Protect the airway first, then build safe mobility and awareness.

items.clinical_focus: Discharge medication reconciliation and readmission prevention

hp.hpi:
Chief Complaint: Discharge teaching before going home.
HPI: Linda Patel is being discharged after heart failure treatment. She has a new diuretic dose, an old bottle of potassium at home, limited transportation, and difficulty reading small print. The nurse must match discharge actions to medication safety, follow-up access, and self-monitoring.
Relevant History: Heart failure, chronic kidney disease stage 3, mild visual impairment, lives alone.

notes.note: Client says, “I have many old pills at home, so I’ll decide which ones look familiar.” She is unsure how to get to the follow-up appointment.

labs.clinical_relevance: Important for diuretic and potassium supplement safety.
Renal function affects medication safety.

orders.order: Medication reconciliation, teach-back, follow-up appointment, daily weights, low-sodium teaching, and home support assessment.
orders.safety_note: Clarify discontinued medications and duplicate therapies.

Review potassium supplements and diuretic dose with current potassium/creatinine results
Assess ability to obtain prescriptions and involve family/home health if appropriate

rationale.answer_analysis: Teach-back with a clear medication list prevents duplicate or discontinued medication use. Appointment and transportation planning support access. Daily weights and symptom reporting support heart failure self-monitoring. Reviewing potassium supplements and diuretic dose with labs protects medication safety and supports HF monitoring. Assessing prescription access and involving supports addresses medication safety and follow-up barriers.
rationale.trap: Do not assume discharge teaching worked without teach-back.
rationale.core_concept: Readmission prevention includes medication clarity, access, and self-monitoring.
rationale.golden_rule: Make the plan usable for the client’s real home situation.
